clue.text: Remove dirt from winding lanes in borders of Cheshire

indicators.note: A winding lane bends one way then another, and letters told to wind will not stay in the order they were handed over.
Whatever is described as in something else sits inside it, so the reshuffled letters land between the pair already found.
The borders of a county are its outer edges, so only the opening and closing letters of the word are wanted.

blocks.note: the outer pair of CheshirE, an English county in the north-west
the five letters of LANES put in a new order

explanation.surface: Scrubbing the mud off twisting country lanes at the edge of Cheshire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Winding lanes' reads as one picture of country roads, and its two words belong to opposite halves of the wordplay: one is the instruction, the other the material.
explanation.definitionFit: Remove dirt from → CLEANSE: the thorough verb for washing a thing clean, stronger than 'clean' and used of wounds and skin.

clue.text: State of agitation about origin of exotic material made from skin

indicators.note: To go about a thing is to go round it, so the word in front closes over the letter named next.
The origin of something is where it begins, so its opening letter is the one taken.

blocks.note: a lather is the froth soap works up, and a person worked up is in one
the first letter of Exotic

explanation.surface: Someone in a flap about where an exotic import came from.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State' looks like the start of a definition — a country, perhaps — and it is nothing of the kind; the definition is the whole tail of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: material made from skin → LEATHER: animal hide tanned into something durable, the everyday name for skin turned into a workable fabric.

clue.text: Permit shown in general lowdown

indicators.note: Something shown in a place is already sitting there, so the letters are read straight out of the words that follow.

blocks.note: the letters sit consecutively across the join between the two words, in the order given

explanation.surface: A permit turning up in the general gossip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lowdown' is the informal word for inside information, which keeps the surface sounding like an office briefing rather than a letter hunt.
explanation.definitionFit: Permit → ALLOW: the verb for letting something happen, matching 'permit' used as a verb rather than the noun for a licence.

clue.text: Celt almost on impulse is cause of great trouble

indicators.note: Almost means falling just short of the whole, so the word gives up its final letter.
In a down clue one thing sitting on another is written above it, so this piece comes first.

blocks.note: a Scot is a Celt, and SCOT written almost to the end stops a letter short
a sudden impulse to do something is the urge to do it

explanation.surface: A Scotsman acting on the spur of the moment and causing havoc.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Celt' names a whole family of peoples and a Scot is only one of them, which is a definition by example and quite fair.
explanation.definitionFit: cause of great trouble → SCOURGE: the word for something that afflicts a whole population, a plague or a pest rather than a minor nuisance.

clue.text: Son slowly moves illegible pieces of handwriting

blocks.note: s is the standard abbreviation for son, the one used on a family tree
traffic that moves slowly crawls

explanation.surface: A boy shifting a pile of unreadable papers at a snail's pace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'S' for son is one of the family abbreviations crosswords lean on constantly, alongside 'w' for wife and 'd' for daughter.
explanation.definitionFit: illegible pieces of handwriting → SCRAWLS: the plural noun for hasty scribbles, writing done too fast for anyone to read.

clue.text: Best shop principally for ointments

indicators.note: Principally means first and foremost, so the leading letter of the word beside it is the one taken.

blocks.note: the cream of something is its best part, as in the cream of the crop
the first letter of Shop

explanation.surface: The best shop to visit if ointment is mainly what you want.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Best' looks like a superlative adjective opening a definition, and it is a noun instead — the cream of the crop.
explanation.definitionFit: ointments → CREAMS: the tubes of medicated preparation rubbed into the skin, the everyday word for such salves.

clue.text: Rent again varying in Spanish-speaking country

indicators.note: Something varying keeps changing, so the letters beside it do not hold the order they were given in.

blocks.note: the nine letters that get reordered

explanation.surface: Rents going up and down again in a country where Spanish is spoken.
explanation.walkthrough: Plenty of countries speak Spanish, so the definition can only point at one of them; the enumeration and the letters settle which.
explanation.definitionFit: Spanish-speaking country → ARGENTINA: one instance of many such countries, the South American republic whose national language is Spanish.

clue.text: Was dishonest about US college of a narrow nature

indicators.note: To be about a thing is to be round it, so the word in front wraps itself over the letters named next.

blocks.note: somebody who was dishonest lied
MIT is the Massachusetts Institute of Technology

explanation.surface: Telling lies about an American university, in a small-minded sort of way.
explanation.walkthrough: MIT is the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, the American college crosswords reach for whenever three letters are needed.
explanation.definitionFit: of a narrow nature → LIMITED: restricted in scope and kept within bounds, the adjective for an outlook or a supply that does not stretch far.

clue.text: Barrier between properties beyond furnace needs rebuilding

indicators.note: A thing that needs rebuilding has to go up again out of the very same parts, put together in a different arrangement.

blocks.note: the thirteen letters that get reordered

explanation.surface: The wall just past the boiler is falling down and has to be put up again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Needs rebuilding' does double duty: in the surface a real structure is coming apart, and in the wordplay it is the letters that must be reassembled.
explanation.definitionFit: Barrier between properties → BOUNDARY FENCE: the fence standing on the line that divides one plot of land from the next.

clue.text: Lack success following trouble

blocks.note: f. is the abbreviation for 'following' used in page references
to trouble somebody is to ail them, as in 'what ails you?'

explanation.surface: Coming to grief in the wake of some trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Following' looks like a positional instruction telling you where the next piece goes, and it is a letter of the answer in its own right.
explanation.definitionFit: Lack success → FAIL: the ordinary verb for coming up short of what was attempted, not the narrower school sense of a failed exam.

clue.text: Cricket side with individual batters lately plucky and playing well

indicators.note: Lately points at the latter end of things, so the closing letter of the word before it is the one taken.

blocks.note: in cricket the on side, or leg side, is the half of the field behind the batter's legs
an individual is a single one
the last letter of batterS
somebody game for anything is plucky

explanation.surface: A cricket team whose batters have lately been brave and in good form.
explanation.walkthrough: Cricket fills the surface and only its first two words are cricketing wordplay; 'batters' is there for its final letter alone.
explanation.definitionFit: playing well → ON ONE'S GAME: the sporting idiom for somebody performing at their best, in the form they are capable of.

clue.text: Group not up to much in brief fall of rain

blocks.note: British slang, out of forces use, for a collection of useless people
read straight: a short burst of wet weather that soon passes over

explanation.surface: A useless crowd caught out in a quick downpour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What a shower!' is the British insult behind the first half, a hopeless rabble, and the weather filling the rest of the clue keeps it out of sight.
explanation.definitionFit: Group not up to much → SHOWER: British slang for a hopeless rabble; brief fall of rain → SHOWER, the short burst of wet weather.

clue.text: Put forward number in team possibly

indicators.note: Possibly says the letters beside it could come out in any arrangement, not only the one printed.

blocks.note: no. is the standard short form for number
the six letters of IN TEAM put in a new order

explanation.surface: Suggesting a squad number for somebody who might make the team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number in team' reads as the digit on a shirt, and 'possibly' is carrying an instruction rather than hedging about who gets picked.
explanation.definitionFit: Put forward → NOMINATE: to propose a person's name for a post or a prize, the formal verb for putting a candidate up.

clue.text: Bid lawyer formulated to get track for riders

indicators.note: A formula is drawn up by setting its parts out in a chosen order, so the letters beside it are arranged anew.

blocks.note: the nine letters that get reordered

explanation.surface: An offer drawn up by a solicitor that ends up producing a horse trail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bid lawyer' sits together in the surface as an offer somebody drafted, and 'formulated' looks like the rest of that phrase while it is really the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: track for riders → BRIDLEWAY: a British public right of way that horse riders may legally use, named from the bridle they ride with.

clue.text: Attractive bread is baked with glee essentially

indicators.note: Dough goes into the oven one shape and comes out another, so the letters beside it are reshaped too.
The essence of a word sits at its centre, so the middle letters are the ones wanted.

blocks.note: seven of the nine letters that get reordered
the two middle letters of gLEe

explanation.surface: Tempting bread, baked with real joy at the heart of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Baked' belongs to the bread in the surface and to the letters in the wordplay, doing both jobs in the one word.
explanation.definitionFit: Attractive → DESIRABLE: worth wanting, the adjective an estate agent reaches for about a house people would like to own.

clue.text: Secure day avoiding area affected by gusts?

indicators.note: To avoid something is to keep clear of it, so the letter named is left out of the word in front.

blocks.note: to secure a prize is to win it
area is A, and DAY with that letter kept out leaves D…Y

explanation.surface: Getting hold of a safe day out, keeping clear of the region the gales are hitting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Area' is A in crossword shorthand, out of maps and mathematics, and here it is a letter to take away rather than one to add.
explanation.definitionFit: affected by gusts? → WINDY: exposed to strong blowing wind, the adjective for a day or a hillside the wind keeps hitting.

clue.text: Secret consignment put in chest as highlighted

indicators.note: Something put in a place ends up inside it, so the letters are sitting inside the words that follow.

blocks.note: the letters run consecutively from inside the first word across the two after it

explanation.surface: A smuggled parcel packed into a chest, exactly as the marking showed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Secret' describes the consignment in the surface and describes what the wordplay has done with the letters, the one adjective covering both.
explanation.definitionFit: Secret consignment → STASH: a quantity of something hidden away, the word for a hoard of drugs or loot kept out of sight.

clue.text: A first sign of visitor in nature walk in ordeal

indicators.note: The first sign of something is the earliest hint of it, so only the opening letter of the word is taken.
Whatever is in something else sits inside it, so these letters are planted in the middle of the word beside them.

blocks.note: a marked nature walk through a wood is a trail
the letter A, lifted straight off the front of the clue
the first letter of Visitor

explanation.surface: Spotting the season's first visitor on a nature walk turns into a slog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A' is usually just the article holding a surface upright, and here it is a letter of the answer in its own right.
explanation.definitionFit: ordeal → TRAVAIL: painful and laborious effort, the older word for toil hard enough to count as suffering.

clue.text: Dub a lefty misguided through lack of positive action?

indicators.note: Somebody misguided has been led the wrong way, and letters led the wrong way come out in the wrong order.

blocks.note: the nine letters that get reordered

explanation.surface: Writing off a left-winger as thoroughly misguided.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dub' is the verb for giving somebody a name, which is what makes the surface read as name-calling rather than as nine letters to reorder.
explanation.definitionFit: through lack of positive action? → BY DEFAULT: describing what comes about simply because nobody did anything to prevent it.

clue.text: Cover even stewed prune

indicators.note: Long stewing breaks a thing down until its pieces sit in the pot every which way, and the letters beside it change places the same way.

blocks.note: the four letters of EVEN put in a new order
to prune a branch is to lop it off

explanation.surface: Putting a lid on a dish of stewed prunes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prune' is a gardener's verb here, not the dried fruit that the stewing beside it points at.
explanation.definitionFit: Cover → ENVELOP: to wrap something up completely, the verb behind the envelope that closes right round a letter.

clue.text: Turn in more extensive comfortable chair

indicators.note: A thing put in another sits inside it, so this letter goes into the middle of the word beside it.

blocks.note: something more extensive in space or in time is longer
a U-turn is the turn you make to double back, so a turn is U

explanation.surface: Swivelling round in a bigger, comfier armchair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn in' opens as one phrase — going to bed, or handing something over — and its two words are doing quite different jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: comfortable chair → LOUNGER: the long padded chair you stretch out on beside a pool, named for the lounging done in it.

clue.text: Unnerve judge describing case for trial

indicators.note: To describe a circle is to draw one round something, so the word in front goes around the letters named next.
A case is the shell a thing sits in, so the outside letters of the word are what is wanted.

blocks.note: to judge a performance is to rate it
the first and last letters of TriaL

explanation.surface: A judge outlining the case that is about to come to trial.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all courtroom, and the only legal word doing wordplay is 'judge'; 'trial' is in the clue for its outside letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Unnerve → RATTLE: to shake somebody's composure until they lose their nerve, the verb for putting a person off their stride.

clue.text: A grim era sadly for union

indicators.note: Sadly says things have gone badly for the words beside it, and letters things have gone badly for do not keep their order.

blocks.note: the eight letters that get reordered

explanation.surface: Looking back sadly on a bleak stretch of history.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Union' pulls towards trade unions in a clue this gloomy, and the older sense — two people joined — is the one wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: union → MARRIAGE: the joining of two people in law, 'union' as a formal bond rather than a workers' organisation.

clue.text: Mist in Virginia – and rain

blocks.note: VA is the postal abbreviation for the state of Virginia
when it rains hard it pours

explanation.surface: Fog hanging over Virginia, followed by heavy rain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rain' is a verb here, which is why it can sit at the end of the clue and still be wordplay rather than a second definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Mist → VAPOUR: water hanging in the air as a fine cloud, 'mist' in its physical, steam-like sense.

clue.text: Old man leading name in charge produces alarm

indicators.note: Whatever leads goes at the front of the line, so this piece is written before the rest.

blocks.note: pa is the familiar word for a father
n is the standard abbreviation for name
i/c is the services' short form for the person in charge

explanation.surface: Dad taking charge and causing a scare.
explanation.walkthrough: Three short conventions stack up in a row — a father, a name and a rank — and the smooth surface hides every join.
explanation.definitionFit: alarm → PANIC: sudden fright that takes hold and spreads, 'alarm' at its most uncontrolled rather than a mild worry.

clue.text: Southern sailor, one in Baltic at work, has period of leave

indicators.note: Letters described as at work are busy doing something, and what they are busy doing here is taking up new places.

blocks.note: s is the standard abbreviation for southern
an AB is an able seaman, the Royal Navy rating crosswords use for any sailor
one is A, and the letters of A BALTIC come out in a new order

explanation.surface: A southern seaman working somewhere in the Baltic earns himself some time off.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is entirely nautical and 'Baltic' is the one sea word in it contributing letters rather than meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: period of leave → SABBATICAL: the stretch of paid leave a university grants a scholar, originally one year in every seven.

clue.text: Badgers and horses in poor condition

blocks.note: the verb: keeps on at somebody until they give in
read straight: worn-out old animals fit for very little

explanation.surface: Badgers alongside a few broken-down horses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Badgers' reads as the striped animals, matching the horses beside it, and it is the verb — to badger somebody is to keep on at them.
explanation.definitionFit: Badgers → NAGS: pesters somebody over and over; and horses in poor condition → NAGS, the dismissive word for tired old horses.

clue.text: One covertly placed in overnight train

blocks.note: an agent planted inside an organisation and left dormant for years
the night service with berths, where you book a bunk rather than a seat

explanation.surface: A spy quietly slipped aboard the night train.
explanation.walkthrough: Both senses come out of lying dormant: one waits years for orders, the other carries passengers who are asleep.
explanation.definitionFit: One covertly placed → SLEEPER: an agent planted long in advance and left inactive; overnight train → SLEEPER, the service with berths for the night.

clue.text: Special form of therapy to do with ghostly figure

blocks.note: sp is the standard short form for special
ECT is electroconvulsive therapy, the shock treatment
re means concerning, as at the head of a memo

explanation.surface: A specialised course of treatment for somebody who keeps seeing an apparition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Special' looks like an adjective describing the therapy, and it is a piece of the answer on its own; the clue holds back its definition until the last two words.
explanation.definitionFit: ghostly figure → SPECTRE: an apparition, the literary word for a ghost seen as a shape rather than felt as a presence.
